newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech bank probe seen sign of govt fight on crime.
newsitem.headline: Czech bank probe seen sign of govt fight on crime.

text.p: A high-profile probe into alleged fraud at IPB bank is a welcome sign that Czech authorities are addressing investor concerns over the lack of tranparency in capital markets, analysts said on Friday.

Investigators earlier this week charged the director and his deputy at IPB, the country's third largest bank by basic capital, with fraud. The bank's supervisory board said the whole affair was based on a misunderstanding.

"It is generally good news for the capital markets," said Jack Schrantz, head of research at Raifeissen Capital and Investment Prague. "It is partially a response to the perception by the public that the ministry of finance has done nothing so far," he added.
Earlier in April, investigators charged 11 people with fraud and related offences in connection with an alleged 137 million crown fraud at troubled Agrobanka a.s..
"I think the attitude is changing fundamentally," said Jan Sykora of brokers Wood and Company.
Foreign and domestic investors have long complained of a lack of transparency in Czech capital markets and of the authorities' failure to tackle the problem.
"There is a perception by foreign investors that this is an insiders' market," said Schrantz.
Investor concerns were highlighted at last month's annual meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.

"Clearly there is an opportunity for the Czech Republic to regulate a bit more carefully the financial sector so that people are better protected from fraud and misrepresentation," first Vice-president Ron Freeman said.
In early April, Deputy Finance Minister Vladimir Rudlovcak, responsible for capital markets, resigned to be replaced by Jiri Spicka, director of the ministry's finance and banking section.
Criticism of Rudlovcak had been mounting after several cases where Czech investment fund managers and major shareholders were found to have been stripping fund assets.

Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's three-party centre-right coalition signalled its intention to tackle the issue last month when, as part of a package of measures to kick-start the economy, it said it would set up an inter-ministerial team to fight crime in the markets.
It proposed a law to create a special body to fight crime in the banking sector, in particular, and promised an investigation into delays in prosecuting economic crime.
Analysts said the government's plan to sell-off the state's 36 pct stake in IPB, and ultimately to complete privatisatiin of the sector, may also have helped prompt the probe.
Klaus said on Wednesday that the government remained committed to the IPB stake sell-off.
"It is extremely crucial to do this one right and if there is something not transparent or suspicious that will not help," said Sykora.
The central bank (CNB) said in March it had divided Agrobanka's assets into sound and questionable portions and that it would sell the sound asets to a strategic investor.
Agrobanka was put under "temporary" forced administration by the CNB last September after running into liqudity problems stemming from the failure of another Czech bank, Kreditni Banka a.s..
